html:
The Cheyenne are an Indigenous people of the Great Plains of North America who speak an Algonquian language. They formed from two tribes, the Tsitsistas and the Suhtai, which merged in the early 1800s.

When Europeans first met them, the Cheyenne lived in what is now Minnesota, as farmers and hunters of the woodlands. Pushed west by other tribes, by the early 1700s they had crossed the Missouri into the Dakotas. There they took up the horse and became bison hunters of the open plains (see horses on the Plains). Settling around the Black Hills and the Powder River country, they introduced horse culture to the Lakota around 1730.

They were close allies of the Arapaho and loosely aligned with the Lakota. As American settlers and soldiers pushed west, the Cheyenne fought for their land. Soldiers killed peaceful Southern Cheyenne families at the Sand Creek massacre in 1864. Northern Cheyenne fought beside the Lakota at the Little Bighorn in 1876. By the end of the 1870s they had been forced onto reservations.

Today they form two nations: the Southern Cheyenne, enrolled with the Arapaho in Oklahoma, and the Northern Cheyenne in Montana.
